Round 1 · 6 possible points

Notice the event and join in

Recall from the lecture

Visual processing, attention and coordinated action depend on interacting regions. White matter connects the nodes. Brainstem arousal systems support all of these steps.

Lecture slides and key terms
  • Slide 18: Frontal systems and control processes
  • Slide 19: Parietal and distributed attention systems
  • Slide 21: Occipital cortex and visual pathways
  • Slide 24: Basal ganglia and internal capsule
  • Slide 25: Brainstem and cerebellum
  • Slide 26: White matter and disconnection

Node: a contributing region. Tract: a connecting white-matter pathway. Association fibres connect regions in one hemisphere; commissural fibres connect hemispheres; projection fibres connect cortex with deeper or lower structures.

You arrive at a campus exhibition. A red star on a crowded poster leads you to a demonstration. The presenter tosses you a soft ball and invites you to take part. Follow the brain systems that make this ordinary sequence possible.

Choose the best set of contributors from the lecture, not a single “brain centre”. No option is an exhaustive list of every region involved; arousal and blood supply support the whole story.

1. Spot the sign

You spot the red star among competing shapes, recognise it, and shift your attention towards it.

2. Catch the ball

The ball approaches. You watch its position, reach, and adjust your hand smoothly to catch it.

3. Hold the instruction and continue

After the catch, you briefly keep the presenter’s next instruction in mind and decide to continue with the demonstration.

Round 2 · 5 possible points

Turn the experience into a memory

Recall from the lecture

The hippocampal–diencephalic system supports new event learning. Frontal strategies influence organisation and retrieval. The fornix and other pathways connect memory-related nodes. These networks also require a continuous blood supply.

Lecture slides and key terms
  • Slide 18: Frontal systems and control processes
  • Slide 20: Medial temporal and diencephalic memory
  • Slide 23: Thalamic circuits and strategic lesions
  • Slide 26: White matter and disconnection
  • Slide 27: Blood supply: the two arterial routes
  • Slide 28: Cerebral arterial territories
  • Slide 29: Deep vessels, border zones and veins
  • Slide 30: Vascular injury and cautious inference

Declarative learning: learning information or events that can later be consciously recalled. Diencephalic: involving deep structures including thalamic and hypothalamic regions. Encoding: processing information as it is learned. Retrieval: accessing learned information.

The demonstration has a surprising ending. The presenter introduces herself as Mei, gives you a short code to repeat, and explains how the trick works. You organise the steps so you can tell a friend later. The story now moves from participating to learning an event.

Choose the best set of contributors from the lecture, not a single “brain centre”. No option is an exhaustive list of every region involved; arousal and blood supply support the whole story.

Round 3 · 5 possible points

Return to the story: what makes remembering possible?

Recall from the lecture

New learning, brief maintenance and strategic retrieval can dissociate. Similar memory difficulties can arise from damage at different nodes or from disconnection. A behavioural result rarely identifies one unique structure.

Lecture slides and key terms
  • Slide 18: Frontal systems and control processes
  • Slide 20: Medial temporal and diencephalic memory
  • Slide 22: Specialisation, lateralisation and inference
  • Slide 23: Thalamic circuits and strategic lesions
  • Slide 26: White matter and disconnection
  • Slide 31: Reasoning checkpoint

Immediate span: briefly maintaining a short sequence. Episodic memory: remembering an event. Disconnection: impaired communication between regions because a pathway is disrupted. A dissociation is a difference between abilities that need not fail together.

The next day, a friend asks about the exhibition. You bring back the room, Mei and the ending, and organise the story into words. Now change one part of your network map at a time to explain what “remembering” depends on.

Choose the best set of contributors from the lecture, not a single “brain centre”. No option is an exhaustive list of every region involved; arousal and blood supply support the whole story.

Anatomical and vascular reference

Use the labels freely. Use these figures alongside the lecture and BrainFacts. Points reward a defensible explanation, not an isolated label.

Memory system and thalamic neighbourhood

The figures locate nodes. Use Morgan Chapter 6 to trace connecting pathways. A memory circuit extends beyond the hippocampus, and the classical Papez route is one organising scaffold within a larger network.

Cortical landmarks, basal ganglia and internal capsule neighbourhood
DistributionAnatomical contextReasoning implication
ACAMainly medial frontal and parietalConsider leg representation and initiation systems
MCAMuch lateral cortex and deep branchesLanguage, attention and motor effects depend on side and branch
PCAMuch occipital and inferomedial temporal tissue; deep branchesVisual and memory effects depend on involved structures
PerforatorsDeep nuclei and white matterA strategic lesion may disrupt a large network
Border zonesBetween major territoriesConsider perfusion and lesion distribution
Arterial routes, collateral links and venous drainage

Internal carotids give rise to ACA and MCA. Vertebral arteries unite as basilar, which usually ends in PCAs. Communicating arteries provide potential collateral routes, with anatomical variation. The MCA is not a segment of the circle of Willis. Veins drain through dural sinuses towards internal jugular veins, following a different organisation from arterial territories.

Debrief: connect the whole story

Trace the story from visual selection to action, new learning and later recall. Name contributing nodes and connecting pathways. Explain why one remembered event cannot be assigned to a single brain centre, and why immediate repetition need not prove successful new learning.
